name: Jeff Bezos
title: The Bookseller Who Reached for Space
subtitle: From a breakfast shift at McDonald's to a garage near Seattle, the everything store and a rocket company: how Jeff Bezos thinks, bets and sometimes gets it wrong.
hook: In 2013, a deep-sea team led by Jeff Bezos lifted the wreckage of Apollo rocket engines from more than ==14,000 feet== under the Atlantic. Months later, conservators cleaning off the corrosion found a serial number, 2044. It matched Engine No. 5 from **Apollo 11**, the Moon launch Bezos had watched on TV when he was five years old.

contact.howToReach: Jeff Bezos stopped running Amazon day to day in 2021, so no route reaches him personally, but some doors into his world are real. If you are an Amazon customer with a genuine problem, jeff@amazon.com is the one address he made public himself; he has said he still sees many of those emails, and he is famous for forwarding some to the right team with a single "?" added, so send one short, specific message with your order number and the fix you want. Journalists should use the press emails of Amazon, the Bezos Earth Fund or Bezos Academy, and shareholders should use Amazon Investor Relations; none of these inboxes are for startup pitches, job requests or fan mail. The Day 1 Families Fund says expert advisors help select its grantees and lists no public application form, so a cold request for money will not work. The Bezos Family Foundation, created by his parents, warns that the "Jeff Bezos Families Relief Fund" promising cash to random people is a scam: never pay, or share personal details with, anyone offering Bezos money.

chapters.title: A Teenage Mom, a Cuban Dad and a Ranch

blocks.text: On ==12 January 1964==, a baby boy was born in Albuquerque, New Mexico. His name was not Bezos yet. On his birth certificate he was Jeffrey Preston Jorgensen.

His mother, Jackie Gise, was ==17== and a junior in high school when he arrived. His father, Ted Jorgensen, was a teenager too, an expert unicycle rider who performed with a local circus. The two had married after Jackie got pregnant. She was 16 on her wedding day.
I can assure you that being a pregnant teenager in high school was not cool in Albuquerque, New Mexico, at that time.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos, interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner, 2018

blocks.text: At first, the school told Jackie she could not finish. She kept pushing back until it gave in. But it let her return only on strict conditions, and decades later she listed them in a graduation speech. Jeff said his grandfather “went to bat for her” when the school tried to throw her out.

For example: Jackie had to arrive and leave within five minutes of the school bells. She was not allowed to talk to other students or eat lunch in the cafeteria. And she was told she could not walk across the stage with her class to collect her diploma.
She was 17. Imagine your own junior year, with a baby.

The marriage did not last. In Brad Stone's account, Ted drank, stayed out late, dropped out of college and did not look for work. About 17 months after Jeff was born, Jackie filed for divorce. Later Ted said it plainly: “I wasn't a good father or a husband.”

Jackie found work as a secretary, even though, in her words, she was a terrible typist who could not read her own shorthand. The job paid ==$190 a month==. That paid for a small apartment for her and her son, but not for a telephone. So her father gave her a walkie-talkie and told her to check in every morning at 7 a.m.

She also refused to stop studying. Jackie signed up for night school and chose classes by one rule: would the professor let her bring a baby? She arrived with Jeff and two duffel bags, one full of textbooks and the other full of cloth diapers, bottles and toys to keep him quiet for a few minutes.

blocks.text: The boy from Cuba in a coat made of rags

In one of those night classes, Jackie met a young Cuban refugee named Miguel “Mike” Bezos. His story was as tough as hers. In ==1962==, at 16, Mike flew alone from Cuba to Miami. He spoke almost no English. His parents sent him away because, under Fidel Castro, they felt they had to protect him.
My parents were not allowed to go into the airport with me, so they dropped me off. I got on an airplane and landed in Miami 45 minutes later.

He was allowed to carry three pairs of pants, three shirts, three pairs of underwear and one pair of shoes. His mother thought America must be freezing, so she and Mike's sister stitched him a heavy coat out of cleaning rags and knitting wool. The Bezos family still has it. Mike was one of about 14,000 young people who fled Cuba to the US in the early 1960s.

Mike spent three weeks in Camp Matecumbe, a refugee camp in Florida. Then he was sent to high school in Wilmington, Delaware, where he won a scholarship to college in Albuquerque. “I had very little idea at that time where Albuquerque was,” he said later. That is the city where he met Jackie and her little boy.
The man who raised him arrived with one pair of shoes.

Jackie married Mike in 1968, when Jeff was four. Mike legally adopted him, and Jeffrey Jorgensen became Jeff Bezos. Jackie had asked Ted to stay out of their lives, and he agreed. Over the years he lost track of the family completely.
The only time I ever think about it, genuinely, is when a doctor asks me to fill out a form.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos on his biological father, to Wired in 1999 (as quoted by The Guardian)

blocks.text: Ted's side of the story has a strange ending. In late 2012 the journalist Brad Stone, researching his book on Amazon, walked into Ted's bike shop in Glendale, Arizona. Ted had no idea who his son had become. Stone had to show him photos on a phone, and he later wrote that Ted's eyes filled with “sorrow and disbelief.” Ted died in 2015.

Mike finished his degree and became an engineer for Exxon, and the family moved to Houston, Texas. Jeff soon had a younger sister, Christina, and a brother, Mark, five and six years younger than him. Jeff has always called Mike his father.
Summers on Grandpa's ranch

Jackie's father, Lawrence Preston Gise, was a serious man with a serious job. He had been a regional director of the US Atomic Energy Commission in Albuquerque, and The Atlantic reports he worked on missile-defence systems for the Pentagon and supervised nuclear labs. He retired early to the family's ==25,000-acre== ranch near Cotulla, a small town in South Texas.
From the age of four, Jeff spent every summer there, three months a year. At first it was partly to give his young parents a break. His grandfather made the little boy feel useful anyway.
He created the illusion for me when I was 4 years old that I was helping him on the ranch. Which, of course, cannot have been true. But I believed it.

Cotulla had about 3,000 people and a tiny Carnegie-style library, smaller than a classroom. By pure luck, one local resident had been a science-fiction fan and donated a whole collection. That is where Jeff fell for Heinlein and Asimov, a love he says never ended. On slow days he also watched soap operas with his grandmother.

photo.caption: The Nueces River running low through Cotulla, Texas, the small ranch town where Jeff spent every summer from age 4 to 16. Photographed in 2009.
photo.author: Billy Hathorn

blocks.text: The day he made his grandmother cry

Some summers his grandparents hitched up their Airstream trailer and joined a caravan club on long road trips across America. Jeff, about 10, sat in the back seat. His grandmother smoked constantly, and he hated the smell. On the radio, anti-smoking ads were claiming that every puff cost you a few minutes of life.
So the boy who loved numbers did the maths in the back seat. Proud of himself, he announced: “At two minutes per puff, you've taken nine years off your life!” His grandmother burst into tears.

His grandfather pulled the car over and took Jeff outside, away from her. Jeff was scared. His grandfather had never said a cross word to him. But he wasn't angry. He just said one sentence that Jeff never forgot.
You're going to figure out one day that it's harder to be kind than clever.
blocks.who: Lawrence Preston Gise, Jeff's grandfather, as Jeff retold it in 2018

blocks.text: Thirty-six years later, in 2010, Jeff built his whole speech to Princeton's graduating class around that moment. His line was simple: “Cleverness is a gift, kindness is a choice.” __Being smart came easily to him; the lesson was that being right and being good are not the same thing.__
Read this twice. Being right is not the same as being kind.
Science fair central

Even as a toddler, Jeff took his crib apart with a screwdriver. The Guardian reports he wanted to sleep in a real bed. As he grew, he rigged an electric alarm to keep his younger brother and sister out of his room and turned the family garage into a lab.

He booby-trapped the house so often that his parents worried, he joked, that one day they would open a door and get ==30 pounds of nails== on their heads. His mother drove him to the RadioShack electronics store again and again for parts.
Okay. Look. Will you please get your parts list straight before we go? I can't handle more than one trip to Radio Shack per day.
blocks.who: Jackie Bezos to young Jeff, as he remembered it

blocks.text: In fourth grade, around ==1974==, his Houston school got something almost no school had: a teletype machine linked by phone to a mainframe computer. A Houston company had donated spare computer time. None of the teachers knew how to use it, so Jeff and a couple of other kids stayed after class and taught themselves to program from the manuals.

For example: after about a week of serious programming, the kids found that someone had already loaded a Star Trek game onto the mainframe. From then on, that is all they did. In playground games of Star Trek, everyone wanted to be Spock or Captain Kirk. Jeff's third choice was the ship's computer. Friends would call “Computer?” and he would answer “Working.”

photo.caption: A Teletype ASR-33 at the Computer History Museum. Jeff learned to program on a school teletype like this one, dialling into a mainframe with a phone handset.
photo.author: ArnoldReinhold

blocks.text: Jackie fought for his schooling the way she had fought for her own. She drove him 40 miles a day so he could attend a Houston elementary school for high-scoring kids. When a waiting list kept him out of the gifted track in middle school, she kept pressing officials until they made an exception.

Here is a real secret from those years. A 1977 book about gifted education in Texas, Turning On Bright Minds, profiled a sixth-grader in a Houston gifted programme called “Tim.” Brad Stone later revealed that “Tim” was Jeff Bezos. The author found him “friendly, but serious,” and his teachers said he was “not particularly gifted in leadership.”
Teachers said: not a leader. He became one. Labels at 12 are not destiny.

He read constantly. In fourth grade he read about ==30 Newbery Award winners== in one year for a class contest, and still lost to someone who read more. His favourite was A Wrinkle in Time. Being sent to his room was no punishment, because he just read. The only time he got in trouble was losing his library privileges for laughing too loudly.

At about six he wanted to be an archaeologist, “before Indiana Jones,” he points out. Then he wanted to be an astronaut. He says he has been thinking about space since he was five. His heroes were Thomas Edison, the inventor, and Walt Disney, who could get huge teams to share one big vision.

blocks.text: Later, Jeff explained what this childhood really gave him. It was not money; the family started with very little. It was people who had his back. __When you know someone loves you no matter what, he argued, you can afford to take big risks.__

Jackie never stopped teaching. Years later she and Mike co-founded the Bezos Family Foundation, and she spent her time there on early learning and how young children's brains develop. She died in 2025. Her own line could sum up her life: “I've devoted my life to providing opportunities for others to learn.”
Lesson: build your safety net of people before you take big risks.

When Jeff was a teenager, the family moved again, this time to Miami, Florida. It was the same city where Mike had landed alone as a refugee years before. Jeff enrolled at Miami Palmetto Senior High School.

By his own account, he was not a cool kid. He calls himself “a very nerdy and good student” who did his homework on time and liked school. He also had a famously loud laugh that he says he has had all his life. For a while, his brother and sister refused to go to the movies with him because it was too embarrassing.
When I was 15, and they were 10 and 9, I had no time for them whatsoever.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos on his younger siblings, 2001

blocks.text: Honest: even future billionaires find little siblings annoying.
The ranch stops being pretend

Every summer until he was 16, Jeff still went back to the ranch in Cotulla. By then the “helping” was real. He and his grandfather did their own veterinary work on the cattle, fixed windmills, laid water pipes, and built fences and barns. The Atlantic adds that he helped castrate bulls.

The big job was the bulldozer, a D-6 Caterpillar. When it broke, they repaired it themselves. The gears were huge, so they built their own cranes just to lift them out. When an animal got sick, his grandfather did not call a vet either. He worked out what to do himself.
I could fix prolapsed cattle; we did all our own veterinary work. Some of the cattle even survived.

Asked what the ranch taught him, Jeff gave a short answer: “Being resourceful. If there's a problem, there's a solution.” But he added a twist he learned later in business. __Doing everything yourself works on a ranch; building a company means making a whole team resourceful, not just you.__

photo.caption: The town sign of Cotulla, Texas, home of his grandfather's ranch. Photographed in 2011.
photo.author: Billy Hathorn

blocks.text: Step one: solve it yourself. Step two: teach a team to.
The breakfast shift at McDonald's

At ==16==, Jeff got his first job: short-order cook on the breakfast shift at a Miami McDonald's, starting before sunrise. He worked strictly in the kitchen and never on the cash registers. The hardest part, he said, was keeping up during the morning rush.

For example: his favourite shift was Saturday morning. “The first thing I would do is get a big bowl and crack 300 eggs into it,” he recalled. One gift the job gave him, he said, was the ability to crack eggs with one hand.

His first week did not go smoothly. A five-gallon ketchup dispenser on the wall got stuck open and dumped ketchup into every hard-to-reach corner of the kitchen. As the new kid, Jeff was handed the cleaning solution and told to get started.
You can learn responsibility in any job, if you take it seriously.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos on his McDonald's job

blocks.text: Future richest man alive, cleaning up ketchup. No job is beneath you.
Computers, teachers and pranks

In 11th grade Jeff got his own computer, an ==Apple II Plus==, and kept tinkering. He credits a run of strong teachers: Mr. Bohr in calculus, Ms. Del Champs in chemistry and Ms. Ruehl in physics. Back in fourth or fifth grade, a maths teacher named Mrs. McInerney had already left a mark.

photo.caption: An Apple II Plus, the computer Jeff got in 11th grade. This one was photographed in 2010.
photo.author: Bilby

blocks.text: He admits he was “unnaturally on the side of not getting in trouble.” In high school he and his friends played pranks, but, he says, the kind that teachers secretly loved. He liked pleasing teachers, and he says great teachers make learning feel so important that you want more of it.

He also had a habit that would later make him rich. He looked at everything around him and saw how it could be better. Even sitting in a restaurant, he would run through ways the place could be improved.
Founders notice what's broken. Train this habit everywhere you go.
The boy who wanted to empty the Earth

His real obsession was space. As a teen he read The High Frontier, a 1976 book by the Princeton physicist Gerard K. O'Neill. It argued that humans could live in giant colonies floating in space. Jeff was hooked by the idea of moving people and heavy industry off the planet.

His high-school girlfriend, Ursula Werner, later said he was not optimistic about what humans were doing to Earth, and that was before global warming was a big public issue. He was also, she said, “really intrigued by the idea of rocketing into outer space.” Years later, reporters tracked her down and she put it even more bluntly.
The reason he's earning so much money is to get to outer space.

In ==1982== Jeff graduated as valedictorian, the top student in his class at Miami Palmetto. He used his graduation speech to describe millions of people moving to colonies in space. The Miami Herald interviewed the 18-year-old about his plans.

For example: he told the Herald he wanted to “build space hotels, amusement parks and colonies for 2 million or 3 million people who would be in orbit.” His reason: “The whole idea is to preserve the Earth.” The paper summed up his goal as turning Earth into “a huge national park.”

blocks.text: Most teenage dreams fade. This one did not. In 2000 he founded a private rocket company, Blue Origin, to make space travel cheaper, and it still runs on the same idea he described at 18. __The thing you are obsessed with at 17 can quietly become the work of your life.__
Write down your 17-year-old dream. Check it again at 35.

There is a fair criticism here too. Jeff was book-smart and knew it. “I have always been academically smart,” he told an audience in Washington in 2018. By his own telling he also had little time for the people around him, like the younger siblings he tried to shut out of his room. The grandfather who taught him kindness had spotted that weak side early. Princeton would test the strong side.

chapters.title: From Physics Dream to the Drive West

blocks.text: In 1982, Jeff arrived at Princeton University in New Jersey. He went there mainly because he wanted to study physics, and Princeton was one of the best places in the world to study physics.

Things went well until quantum mechanics. By then about 30 students were left in the class. Jeff was still getting good grades, but every problem was a slog. He watched three or four classmates absorb ideas easily that took him 12 hours of work.
I realized I'm never going to be a great physicist.

In 2018 he told a funnier version on stage. He had spent three hours stuck on a hard maths problem, a partial differential equation. So he went to the smartest student he knew, Yasantha Rajakarunanayake, a young man from Sri Lanka. Without writing anything down, Yasantha worked out the answer in seconds: cosine.

Then he wrote out three pages of algebra to prove it. Jeff asked if he had done it in his head. No, Yasantha said. He had solved a similar problem three years earlier and simply mapped one onto the other. Jeff called him “the smartest guy at Princeton.”
That was the very moment when I realized I was never going to be a great theoretical physicist.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos at the Economic Club of Washington, 2018

blocks.text: Knowing what you're NOT best at is a superpower. Switch early.

He admits giving up physics was hard; it had been his goal for years. But he was already taking computer science classes and found himself pulled toward them. He learned not just to hack code but the maths and algorithms behind it. __He didn't quit learning; he moved to the field where his talent gave him an edge.__

Space stayed with him. Jeff became president of Princeton's chapter of SEDS, Students for the Exploration and Development of Space, and attended seminars by Gerard O'Neill, the author of the space-colony book he had read as a teen. He graduated in ==1986== with a degree in electrical engineering and computer science.

photo.caption: Jeffrey P. Bezos in the Princeton University yearbook, 1986, the year he graduated at 22.
photo.author: Princeton University

blocks.text: The startup he didn't start

At 22, Jeff already wanted to start a company. He even talked to a couple of friends about it. Then he made a decision that many young founders skip: he decided to wait and learn how business and the world actually worked first.
One of the things that it's very hard to believe when you're 22 or 23 years old is that you don't already know everything.

Instead he joined a young startup in New York called Fitel, which was building a computer network to help brokerage firms clear their trades. He admits it sounds obscure, but it used his technical skills and he loved the people. Then he moved to the bank Bankers Trust and rose to vice president.

From then on he worked where computers meet money. That is how he landed at D. E. Shaw, a New York hedge fund that used computers to trade stocks. As Jeff put it, they programmed the computers, and the computers made the trades.

For example: D. E. Shaw hunted talent by mailing unsolicited letters to top students on the dean's lists of elite universities. The letters said, without embarrassment: “We approach our recruiting in unapologetically elitist fashion.”

The founder, the computer scientist David E. Shaw, had already played with the early internet in the 1980s and saw that it could change business. He gave Jeff the job of finding investment ideas in this new online world. In those years, The Atlantic reports, the two even kicked around the idea of an “everything store.” Jeff rose fast and became a senior vice president.
The Amazon idea came from his day job. Look closely at yours.

Jeff's personal life had a very Jeff-like chapter. Before he met his future wife, The Guardian reports, he tried to apply analytics to dating. He called it “women flow” and thought ballroom dancing might improve his odds. Then, at D. E. Shaw, he interviewed a fellow Princeton graduate, MacKenzie Tuttle, for a job.

MacKenzie later said that she was the one who chased him, not the other way round. Within three months they were engaged, and three months after that they were married. The wedding was in 1993. He was 29.
The number that changed everything

In the spring of 1994, Jeff came across a statistic that stopped him cold. Use of the World Wide Web was growing at about ==2,300 percent a year==. “You know, things just don't grow that fast,” he said later. He started asking which business plan would make sense with growth like that.

Being a methodical quant, he made a list of the top 20 mail-order businesses and asked which could be run better online. Books won. There were millions of titles, so no paper catalogue could ever list them all, but a website could. He flew to Los Angeles for the American Booksellers' convention and learned that the big book wholesalers already kept electronic lists of their stock.

blocks.text: D. E. Shaw did not want to do it, so Jeff decided to do it himself. He went to his boss and said he was going to leave and start a company selling books online. His boss said, “Let's go on a walk.” They walked through Central Park for two hours.
You know, this actually sounds like a really good idea to me, but it sounds like it would be a better idea for somebody who didn't already have a good job.
blocks.who: Jeff's boss at D. E. Shaw, as Jeff recalled it

blocks.text: His boss asked him to think about it for 48 hours. Jeff needed a way to make a decision this big. He invented one and gave it a name that, he joked, “only a nerd would call” it: the regret minimisation framework. He imagined himself at 80, looking back on his life, and asked which choice he would regret.
I knew that if I failed I wouldn't regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not ever having tried.
Very important for first-time founders! Most regrets are things you didn't do.

Then came the family. In 1994, he says, almost everyone's first question was “What's the internet?” MacKenzie, though, was all in from the start: “Great — let's go!” His mother was more cautious. “Don't quit your job,” she warned, and asked whether he could do it on nights and weekends instead.

His father's first question was also “What's the Internet?” Jeff told his parents the honest truth: he thought there was a ==70 percent== chance they would lose every dollar. They invested a large part of their life savings anyway. “As corny as it sounds, we were betting on Jeff,” Mike said later.

For example: Jeff's 70 percent was not pessimism. He reckoned most startups have only about a 10 percent chance of working, so he was giving himself triple the normal odds. Being realistic, he said, took away the fear of failing, because failure was simply the most likely outcome.
The drive west

He chose Seattle. It was close to the giant book wholesaler Ingram and full of computer talent. The Guardian notes a sharper reason too: under US law back then, the company had to collect sales tax only on sales within its own state.

Over the Independence Day weekend of ==July 1994==, Jeff and MacKenzie flew to Texas and picked up a 1988 Chevy Blazer, a gift from Mike. Then they drove across America. MacKenzie drove. Jeff sat beside her and typed the first draft of a 30-page business plan.

From the road, he called a friend in Seattle to recommend a lawyer. The friend suggested his own divorce lawyer, and Jeff took him. When the lawyer asked on the phone what to call the company, Jeff said “Cadabra, as in abra cadabra.” The lawyer replied: “Cadaver?” Jeff knew then it was not going to be a good name. A few months later, it was changed.

He stopped in San Francisco to interview engineers. There he found Shel Kaphan, the programmer who would build the company's early systems and whom Jeff later called the most important person in Amazon's history. __Business plan, lawyer, first hire: none of it was glamorous, but it was all done before the car reached Seattle.__

blocks.text: Look at the order in which Jeff did things. At 22 he wanted to be a founder, but he spent eight more years learning technology and finance first. He jumped only when the data showed a window opening and he had a clear plan for using it. __He didn't wait for courage; he waited until the odds and the timing made sense, then moved fast.__
He was 30 here. Not 19. Late starts are still starts.

In the summer of 1994, a 30-year-old with a good Wall Street job, a new wife and a hand-me-down car rolled into Seattle. His parents were ready to bet their savings on him, and he had a company with a name that sounded like “cadaver.” The real story was about to start, in a garage.

Most biographies give you two names: Amazon and Blue Origin. The real list is longer and much funnier. It starts with a summer camp that signed up six children. It runs through a news service that a bank killed before it began. It includes a phone that sold so badly it was cut to 99 cents, and a health-care company built with Warren Buffett that closed within about three years.

Read this chapter as a scorecard. Each entry shows the idea, the choice behind it, where the first money came from, what happened and what to copy. __Count the failures as you go, because the wins only make sense next to them.__
Twenty-odd ventures. Count how many you had already heard of.
Before Amazon

blocks.name: The DREAM Institute
blocks.idea: A 10-day summer camp for younger children, meant to make them think and read widely. The required reading included Dune, The Lord of the Rings, Gulliver's Travels and Stranger in a Strange Land.
blocks.decision: He had spent a teenage summer working at McDonald's and disliked it. The next summer, instead of finding another job, he and his girlfriend created their own product.
blocks.howStarted: Two teenagers, a reading list and a price. Six children signed up.
blocks.funding: No investors. Parents paid $600 per child. Six children at $600 is $3,600 at most, by our arithmetic.
blocks.whatHappened: It was a tiny one-off, and we found no record of it continuing. Then he left for Princeton. Its real value is what it shows: a teenager who would rather charge for an idea than wait for a wage.
blocks.lesson: Charge real money for your first idea, even if only six people pay. A price tells you more than a compliment.

blocks.name: Worldwatch, the news service with Halsey Minor
blocks.idea: Take several news feeds, sort them by topic and send each banker only the stories that matched their work. Think of a personal news feed, delivered by fax or email, long before most people had a feed at all.
blocks.decision: Bezos was so taken with it that he nearly quit his job at Bankers Trust. Minor had worked at Merrill Lynch, and the pitch to the bank was simple: bankers would value a filter.
blocks.howStarted: Two young men in New York and a partnership, with Merrill Lynch as the planned first customer and backer.
blocks.funding: Merrill was going to put up $750,000, Minor recalled. Forbes reported in 1998 that the bank first approved the project and then pulled the plug. Merrill had lost money in 1990.
blocks.whatHappened: They tried to work out how to raise the money elsewhere. On a phone call, they agreed they could not, and went their separate ways. Minor, crushed, later founded CNET. By 1998 his stake in it was valued at $184 million. Bezos moved on, and four years later he was driving to Seattle.
blocks.lesson: Do not build a startup on one backer's promise. And keep your failures in perspective: both men recovered very well from this one.

blocks.text: The engine

Everything else in this chapter depends on the next entry. Amazon's shares pay for the rockets, and his Amazon wealth bought the newspaper. Amazon's cash paid for most of the other experiments. So we give it the longest entry, and later chapters tell its story scene by scene.

blocks.name: Amazon.com
blocks.idea: An online bookstore with millions of titles, something no physical shop could hold. The internet was growing fast, and he reckoned a store with unlimited shelves could only exist there.
blocks.decision: He made the call, he says, with his heart more than his head, because he expected to regret not trying more than he would regret failing. He avoided Silicon Valley partly because of the sales tax he would have had to charge California shoppers. He then chose Kleiner Perkins over General Atlantic for his venture money.
blocks.howStarted: A garage at a rented three-bedroom house in Bellevue, near Seattle, with desks made from Home Depot doors. Shel Kaphan, the first employee, built the site. It opened on ==16 July 1995== and took $12,000 in orders in its first week. By the end of the first month it had sold to all 50 US states and 45 countries.
blocks.funding: $10,000 of his own for 10.2 million shares, plus $84,000 in interest-free loans he made to the company. Then $245,573 from his parents, about $1 million from around 20 angels, $8 million from Kleiner Perkins and $54 million from the 1997 stock market listing.
blocks.whatHappened: Sales went from $511,000 in 1995 to $15.7 million in 1996, and to ==$716.9 billion== in 2025, with $80 billion in operating profit. It came close to a cash crisis around 2000 and 2001, as the near-death chapter shows. Bezos stepped down as CEO in July 2021 and is now executive chair. Andy Jassy runs it.
blocks.lesson: Pick a narrow first product inside a market that is growing wildly. Books were the door. The everything store came later.

blocks.text: $10,000 in 1994. $716.9 billion in sales in 2025. Same company.
The first big failures

blocks.name: Amazon Auctions and zShops, later Marketplace
blocks.idea: Let other people sell through Amazon. Auctions copied eBay. zShops let small shops sell at fixed prices. Marketplace put outside sellers on the same page as Amazon's own stock.
blocks.decision: eBay was the threat. Fortune noted that Amazon launched auctions two days after eBay announced a share sale. The bigger choice came later. Amazon decided to let rival sellers compete directly beside its own products, even when that took a sale from itself.
blocks.howStarted: Auctions launched in March 1999 and zShops that autumn.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash and borrowings. No separate investors.
blocks.whatHappened: By Bezos's own telling, almost nobody came to Auctions and zShops did little better. The third attempt worked. In 2017 outside sellers passed half of all items sold. By the third quarter of 2026 they were ==61 percent== of units, and seller services brought in $172.2 billion in 2025.
blocks.lesson: A failed product may be the right idea in the wrong shape. Change the form before you throw out the idea.

blocks.text: I think seven people came, if you count my parents and siblings.
blocks.who: Jeff Bezos on Amazon Auctions, 2014 letter to shareholders

blocks.text: Today this brings in over $172 billion a year. Seven people. Read that twice.

blocks.name: The dot-com stakes: Pets.com, Kozmo, drugstore.com, HomeGrocer, living.com and more
blocks.idea: Buy big pieces of other online shops. Amazon would get a share of each new category without building it, and those shops would pay Amazon to promote them.
blocks.decision: Amazon believed the internet was a land rush: grab ground now, make it pay later. In 1999 Fortune counted 46 percent of Drugstore.com, 35 percent of HomeGrocer, 54 percent of Pets.com and 49 percent of Gear.com. Amazon announced a major move about every six weeks that year.
blocks.howStarted: Bezos and his team made these investments in rapid succession during the boom. Partners also agreed to pay fees, such as $105 million over three years from drugstore.com and $145 million over five years from living.com.
blocks.funding: Amazon's stock and the billions it had borrowed. About $57.8 million went into Pets.com, $62.5 million into HomeGrocer and $60 million for 32 percent of Kozmo.
blocks.whatHappened: The bust wiped most of it out. Pets.com closed in November 2000, sacking about 255 of its 320 staff, with $147 million in cumulative losses. Living.com went bankrupt and Kozmo shut in 2001. Amazon recorded $305 million in investment losses in 2000. It kept selling the Pets.com sock puppet at $19.99 even after the company had folded, 100 times the price of a Pets.com share.
blocks.lesson: Owning part of a business does not fix its economics. Check whether each order makes money before you buy in.

blocks.text: For example: Amazon's most consequential small deal of 1998 had an Indian team behind it. Junglee was started in 1996 by Rakesh Mathur and Stanford PhD students, including Anand Rajaraman, Venky Harinarayan and Ashish Gupta. Four of its five founders were of Indian origin. Its software compared prices across websites. Amazon paid about 1.6 million shares. Then Ram Shriram, who was with Junglee at the sale, took Bezos to meet two students named Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

blocks.name: Personal investing and Bezos Expeditions
blocks.idea: Put his own money into young companies and science projects, separate from Amazon. Bezos Expeditions is the name of the vehicle he uses.
blocks.decision: The first famous cheque went to Google in 1998. Asked why, he told author Ken Auletta that he simply fell in love with the two founders. His official list of holdings now includes many AI and robotics firms.
blocks.howStarted: A meeting in a Menlo Park garage in 1998, arranged by Shriram. Bezos was one of only a few early angels.
blocks.funding: His own money. The Google cheque was reported at $250,000, at four cents a share by Auletta's account.
blocks.whatHappened: That cheque became about 3.3 million Google shares at the 2004 IPO. An Amazon spokesman declined to say what he did with them. The official site now lists Airbnb, Uber, Twitter, Workday, Stack Overflow, Remitly, Perplexity, Figure and Physical Intelligence among others. He also backed Cambrian Ventures, the fund of Junglee's Rajaraman and Harinarayan.
blocks.lesson: Your first success opens doors you did not know about. Stay close to the smart people you meet on the way, because the next deal usually comes through them.

blocks.text: The rocket

blocks.name: Blue Origin
blocks.idea: Make getting to space far cheaper by reusing rockets, so that one day heavy industry can move off Earth. He says the point is to protect the planet, and he has wanted this since high school.
blocks.decision: In 1999 he and novelist Neal Stephenson saw the rocket film October Sky and went for coffee. Bezos said he had long wanted a space company, and Stephenson asked why he did not start one that day. The team first explored alternatives to chemical rockets, then decided that conventional rockets, reused, were the right road.
blocks.howStarted: Blue Operations LLC, in a former envelope factory in south Seattle. Stephenson says he was the only employee for a little while. Early members included inventor Danny Hillis, science historian George Dyson and Amazon's general counsel. Workers would tell neighbours only that they did scientific research.
blocks.funding: Bezos alone for 26 years, with small NASA awards of $3.7 million and $22 million along the way. In 2017 he said he was selling about $1 billion of Amazon stock a year to pay for it. The Wall Street Journal, cited by CNBC, puts the total near ==$30 billion==.
blocks.whatHappened: First test hop in November 2006, reaching 285 feet. A vehicle lost in August 2011. First rocket to land after reaching space in November 2015. Bezos flew in July 2021. New Glenn reached orbit in January 2025. In May 2026 a rocket blew up on the pad during a test, and SpaceNews says the rebuilt pad should be ready by the first half of December. That autumn, outside investors came in for the first time at a reported $140 billion.
blocks.lesson: A very long project needs a money machine behind it. He built the machine first, then fed the dream from it.

blocks.text: The bets made with Amazon's money

blocks.name: Amazon Prime
blocks.idea: Pay once a year and get free two-day delivery on everything. All you can eat, for shipping.
blocks.decision: Engineer Charlie Ward first raised the idea of a yearly fee. Bezos added speed to it. The team weighed $49 and $99 before he settled on $79, big enough to matter but small enough to try. Some senior people pushed back hard and told the team it should not let him do this.
blocks.howStarted: A small secret team, code-named Futurama, built it in about six weeks over the 2004 holidays.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash flow. Bezos told customers it would be expensive for Amazon in the short term.
blocks.whatHappened: Launched on 2 February 2005. Tens of thousands signed up in the first month. The price rose to $99 in 2014. Video streaming was added later as a free extra. Subscription services, which include Prime fees, brought in $49.6 billion in 2025.
blocks.lesson: Sell the habit, not the product. Once someone has paid up front, they stop comparing prices elsewhere.

blocks.name: Amazon Web Services
blocks.idea: Rent out computing power and storage over the internet, by the hour, so that anyone could run software without buying servers.
blocks.decision: At a 2003 executive offsite at Bezos's home, his team asked what Amazon was truly good at. Running reliable, cheap data centres came out of that exercise. Fortune calls the decision to sell this to outsiders the turning point, one that could easily have gone the other way.
blocks.howStarted: Andy Jassy wrote the plan, which reportedly went through 31 drafts. Chris Pinkham, who wanted to go home to South Africa, set up a team in Cape Town that built the computing service. By late 2004 a small office of about 14 people was working on it.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash. There was no outside round and no separate company.
blocks.whatHappened: Storage launched in March 2006 and computing that August. Amazon hid the numbers until 2015. In 2025 AWS earned $128.7 billion in sales and $45.6 billion in operating profit. By the third quarter of 2026 it made ==63 percent== of Amazon's operating profit on about 23 percent of its sales.
blocks.lesson: List what you had to get good at to survive. One of those painful skills may be a bigger business than the one you are in.

blocks.name: Kindle and Lab126
blocks.idea: A reading device with a built-in wireless link that could fetch a book in under a minute, so Amazon would own digital books before Apple or Google could.
blocks.decision: In 2004 Bezos took Steve Kessel off the job of running books, which Kessel thought was the best job in the world, and told him to act as if his goal was to put everyone selling physical books out of work. Bezos insisted one person could not run both the old and the new business.
blocks.howStarted: A secret hardware lab called Lab126 in Silicon Valley, led by Palm veteran Gregg Zehr. Amazon had never built hardware. The code name, Fiona, came from a Neal Stephenson novel.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash. Kessel first estimated 18 months and a small team. It took three and a half years and far more people.
blocks.whatHappened: Launched on 19 November 2007 at $399, with 90,000 books, most new titles and bestsellers at $9.99. The first stock sold out in about five and a half hours, and Amazon ran out again the next Christmas.
blocks.lesson: If your business will be disrupted, do it yourself first. And give the new team a boss who has no old business to protect.

blocks.text: Abroad: one retreat, one fight

blocks.name: Amazon China (Joyo)
blocks.idea: Enter the world's most populous market by buying a local online book and media seller.
blocks.decision: Amazon chose to buy rather than build, paying $75 million for Joyo in 2004. Its largest shareholder at the time was Lei Jun, who later founded Xiaomi.
blocks.howStarted: It kept the Joyo business and later rebranded it under the Amazon name.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash.
blocks.whatHappened: It held about 15 percent of the market around 2011 and 2012, and under 1 percent by 2019. Alibaba's Tmall and JD.com controlled 82 percent by then. Amazon closed its China marketplace on 18 July 2019, keeping cross-border sales, Kindle and cloud computing.
blocks.lesson: A global brand does not beat local habits. Payment, delivery and marketing have to fit the country, or a local rival will fit it for you.

blocks.name: Amazon India
blocks.idea: After China, do not lose the last big e-commerce market. Enter India as a marketplace, with Amazon handling the warehousing and delivery for local sellers.
blocks.decision: Indian rules barred foreign-owned online retailers from selling their own stock directly, so Amazon had to use the marketplace model. It sent Amit Agarwal, from Bezos's senior team in Seattle, to lead. It revived the old Junglee name first as a price-comparison site in February 2012.
blocks.howStarted: Amazon.in opened in June 2013 with about 100 sellers, selling only books, films and TV shows, from a warehouse near Mumbai. Flipkart, founded by two former Amazon employees, had a six-year head start.
blocks.funding: Amazon's cash. In July 2014, one day after Flipkart announced a $1 billion raise, Bezos announced $2 billion for India. Amazon spent it in under two years and added $3 billion in 2016.
blocks.whatHappened: Amazon reached 100 million customers by 2018, with annual losses of up to about $1 billion, but still trailed the Flipkart group on gross sales. Walmart bought Flipkart in 2018. Bernstein estimated Amazon had invested around $6.5 billion, with India still unprofitable as of 2023.
blocks.lesson: Money can buy you speed in a price war, but not automatically first place. Your rival can find a bigger backer too.

blocks.text: Flipkart's founders trained at Amazon. Then they made Bezos spend billions.
Bought, not built

blocks.name: Zappos
blocks.idea: The top online shoe seller, famous for customer service and an unusual company culture.
blocks.decision: Bezos visited in 2005 and was told no at any price, by Tony Hsieh's account. Four years later the recession had tightened credit, and Hsieh writes that his board wanted a sale and that he feared being replaced. Amazon agreed to preserve Zappos's independence and culture, and that made a deal possible.
blocks.howStarted: Amazon came back after waiting four years. Zappos was by then doing over $1 billion in gross sales and had leaned on a $100 million credit line for stock.
blocks.funding: About 10 million Amazon shares, plus $40 million in cash and restricted stock for staff. It was worth about $1.2 billion by closing because Amazon's stock rose.
blocks.whatHappened: Zappos still runs as a separate brand. Hsieh's essay remains a warning about how investors can force a founder's hand when credit runs out.
blocks.lesson: Founders: outside money gives outsiders a vote. Buyers: keep what makes the target special, and be ready to wait years.

blocks.name: Quidsi (Diapers.com)
blocks.idea: Marc Lore and Vinit Bharara started Diapers.com in New Jersey in 2005, an online shop built around what new parents buy again and again.
blocks.decision: Amazon slashed its own diaper prices while Quidsi was growing, which squeezed its margins and made investors shy. Brad Stone's book reports that Bezos threatened to take big losses and drive prices towards zero. Quidsi talked to Walmart, and Amazon won the bidding war.
blocks.howStarted: Quidsi was a going business. Amazon bought it in November 2010.
blocks.funding: $545 million from Amazon. The founders had raised money from venture investors, who grew reluctant during the price war.
blocks.whatHappened: Amazon said it could never make the unit profitable, and closed the Quidsi sites in 2017, laying off 263 people. Lore left, built Jet.com and sold it to Walmart for $3.3 billion. The mistakes chapter covers the questions lawmakers later asked about it.
blocks.lesson: If a giant can match your whole product, a price lead will not save you. Build something it cannot copy just by spending.

blocks.name: The Washington Post
blocks.idea: Buy a famous, struggling newspaper personally, give it time and money, and help it find a national digital audience.
blocks.decision: The Graham family had owned it for 80 years. Revenue had fallen for seven years straight, and publisher Katharine Weymouth warned of a possible $40 million loss in 2013. Bankers at Allen & Co. connected the sides, and Graham and Bezos met at the Sun Valley conference in July and quickly agreed. He told staff he could offer financial runway.
blocks.howStarted: A $250 million cash purchase through a company of his own, not Amazon. He kept the senior editors in place.
blocks.funding: His own money. Reuters noted that the price was about four times what comparable newspaper deals suggested.
blocks.whatHappened: The paper had profitable years around the first Trump term. Then it lost $77 million in 2023 and about $100 million in 2024. In February 2026 it cut about a third of its staff. The mistakes chapter tells the wider story.
blocks.lesson: Patient money still needs a working business model. Runway only helps if the plane can eventually fly.

blocks.text: The phone and the voice

blocks.name: Fire Phone
blocks.idea: An Amazon smartphone with a 3D-like display, face-tracking cameras and a free year of Prime.
blocks.decision: Bezos defended it as a bold bet and said a phone would take many tries. Amazon chose an exclusive deal with one US carrier, AT&T, and launched just before Apple's new iPhones.
blocks.howStarted: An internal devices team that grew to as many as 1,000 people, with Ian Freed a key leader.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own money, reported at over $100 million for the team, plus the charge below.
blocks.whatHappened: The $199 price fell to 99 cents with a two-year contract. An estimate put early sales at only 35,000. Amazon took a ==$170 million== charge in October 2014 and stopped selling it by September 2015. That same October, Amazon reported its biggest quarterly loss in 14 years.
blocks.lesson: Do not enter a crowded market with a feature nobody asked for. But do keep the people and the code, because the next bet may need them.

blocks.name: Echo and Alexa
blocks.idea: A speaker you talk to, with its brain in Amazon's cloud. Bezos's stated dream was the talking computer from Star Trek.
blocks.decision: He sketched it himself on a whiteboard in early 2011. He wanted it to cost $20. He picked his technical adviser Greg Hart to lead it, even though Hart said he had no hardware experience. Bezos chose the name, after the ancient library of Alexandria.
blocks.howStarted: A team that grew past 200 people with a budget above $50 million, per The New Yorker. Fire Phone people and lessons fed into it.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own cash.
blocks.whatHappened: Launched quietly on 6 November 2014 with a press release and a short video, not a big stage show. It created a whole category, and Amazon spoke of hundreds of millions of devices by 2020. It also cost a fortune: The Wall Street Journal reported tens of billions lost across the devices unit.
blocks.lesson: A hit product can still be a poor business. Ask how it will make money before you ship a hundred million.

blocks.text: The graveyard

Fire Phone gets the headlines, but the small failures teach you more about how the place ran. People could pitch an idea and build it with very little second-guessing. Most of these experiments quietly died. Bloomberg listed 37 projects killed after Jassy took over in 2021, projects it described as dreamed up during the Bezos era.

blocks.name: The small flops: WebPay, Wallet, Local, Local Register, Destinations, Dash, Restaurants, Halo
blocks.idea: Quick tests, each aimed at a rival's turf: PayPal and Square in payments, Groupon in local deals, Expedia in travel, the delivery apps in restaurant food. Dash was a physical button that reordered one household item. Halo was a health-tracking band.
blocks.decision: Amazon's rule was to try, measure and move on. Bezos has argued that failure and invention are twins, and that a large company should run proportionately large experiments.
blocks.howStarted: Small internal teams. Destinations launched in April 2015. Wallet lasted about six months. Restaurants began in 2015 and reached 20 US cities plus London.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own budget in every case, with amounts rarely made public.
blocks.whatHappened: WebPay closed in 2014 after seven years. Destinations stopped within six months, in October 2015. Local closed that December. Local Register ended in February 2016. Dash buttons stopped in 2019, and Restaurants closed in June 2019. Halo stopped working in August 2023, with Amazon refunding recent buyers.
blocks.lesson: Run cheap experiments, kill them quickly, and make sure the failures are small enough that you can afford many.

blocks.name: Whole Foods Market
blocks.idea: Buy a real-world, upmarket grocery chain with more than 460 stores to push into fresh food.
blocks.decision: Activist investor Jana Partners took a stake of nearly 9 percent in April 2017 and pressed for change. Whole Foods looked for a friendly buyer. Amazon offered $41 a share, Whole Foods asked for $45, and Amazon named $42 as its best and final price.
blocks.howStarted: CEO John Mackey and three executives flew to Seattle for what he called a blind date, arranged through mutual friends. Seven suitors circled in all, and Amazon came close to walking away.
blocks.funding: $13.7 billion, its largest deal ever.
blocks.whatHappened: By January 2026 Amazon reported over 40 percent sales growth and more than 550 stores, with 100-plus new stores planned.
blocks.lesson: When you cannot build the skill fast, buy it. Then know your walk-away price, and name it out loud.

blocks.name: Amazon Go and Amazon Fresh stores
blocks.idea: Shops with no checkout line. You scanned your phone, cameras and sensors watched what you took, and your account was charged when you left. Fresh stores later brought the idea to full supermarkets.
blocks.decision: Amazon wanted a store format of its own to change physical shopping, not just to own Whole Foods.
blocks.howStarted: A 1,800-square-foot shop in Seattle, open to staff from 5 December 2016 and to the public on 22 January 2018.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own budget. It did not disclose the cost.
blocks.whatHappened: In January 2026 Amazon said it had not created a distinctive experience with an economic model that could scale. It closed Go and Fresh stores within days, except in California, where they stayed open longer to meet state rules, and is converting some to Whole Foods. Fresh continues online.
blocks.lesson: Clever technology is not a business model. If the shop does not earn its costs, shoppers' amazement will not save it.

blocks.name: Haven
blocks.idea: Three giants, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway and JPMorgan Chase, jointly tackle employee health-care costs.
blocks.decision: The 2018 announcement was so bold that health-care shares fell. Surgeon and writer Atul Gawande was picked to lead it.
blocks.howStarted: A nonprofit based in Boston, which had 57 staff at the end.
blocks.funding: The three founding companies. The amount has not been disclosed.
blocks.whatHappened: Gawande stepped back in May 2020. Each parent kept running its own projects with its own staff, which left Haven little to do. It closed at the end of February 2021. Bloomberg reported little evidence of new approaches.
blocks.lesson: A partnership of giants needs one clear owner. If everyone also runs their own version, the joint project will die.

blocks.name: Amazon Care
blocks.idea: App-based medical care with video visits and nurses who came to your home, first for Amazon staff in Seattle, then for other employers.
blocks.decision: Test on your own employees first, then sell the service to other companies.
blocks.howStarted: A pilot for Amazon staff around Seattle in 2019.
blocks.funding: Amazon's own budget.
blocks.whatHappened: Few businesses signed up. Amazon said it was not a complete enough offering and ended it on 31 December 2022, cutting 159 jobs, while 236 more went at the contracted clinic. About a month earlier it had agreed to buy One Medical for $3.9 billion.
blocks.lesson: Your own employees are a captive audience. Real customers, who can say no, are the real test.

blocks.text: His own money, his own causes

blocks.name: Bezos Day One Fund and Bezos Earth Fund
blocks.idea: Two giving vehicles. Day One funds groups helping homeless families and runs free preschools. Earth Fund gives grants to fight climate change and protect nature.
blocks.decision: He announced Day One in September 2018, a year after asking for ideas in public, and Earth Fund in February 2020. Each has one defined mission, and Earth Fund has a hard deadline.
blocks.howStarted: Day One's first Bezos Academy preschool opened in Des Moines, Washington, in October 2020. Earth Fund's first $791 million in grants went to 16 groups in November 2020.
blocks.funding: His own money: a $2 billion commitment to Day One and $10 billion to Earth Fund, to be fully given out by 2030.
blocks.whatHappened: Forbes says Earth Fund had granted $2.4 billion as of its latest update. His giving has drawn criticism and praise, covered in the personal-life chapter.
blocks.lesson: Give a cause a deadline and a number. A public target forces you to act.

blocks.name: The 10,000-Year Clock and the Apollo engines
blocks.idea: Two strange projects with no profit in them. One is a giant clock meant to run for 10,000 years, designed by Danny Hillis, to make people think in long time spans. The other was to raise Apollo rocket engines from the sea floor.
blocks.decision: Neither was meant to earn money. Hillis was an early colleague at Blue Origin, and Bezos has dreamed of space since he was five.
blocks.howStarted: The clock is being built inside a mountain on his Texas land. For the engines, he assembled deep-sea explorers, including some who had searched for the Titanic.
blocks.funding: His own money: a reported $42 million for the clock. The engine recovery was privately funded through Bezos Expeditions.
blocks.whatHappened: After three weeks at sea in March 2013, his team lifted parts of two F-1 engines from more than 4 kilometres down. They stayed NASA's property, and restored parts are on show at Seattle's Museum of Flight.
blocks.lesson: Keep something in your life that pays nothing. It is a good test of what you really care about.

blocks.name: Prometheus
blocks.idea: AI for the physical economy: tools to speed up how engineers design and make real things. He calls the goal an artificial general engineer.
blocks.decision: He had worked on it since late 2024, and it became the first CEO job he had taken since leaving that role at Amazon in 2021. He says it now takes the bulk of his time, and says it has nothing to do with robotics.
blocks.howStarted: About 150 people by mid-2026 across San Francisco, London and Zurich, hired from places like OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Nvidia. His co-CEO is Vik Bajaj, who co-founded Alphabet's Verily.
blocks.funding: $6.2 billion at launch in November 2025, with Bezos putting in capital. Then a $12 billion second round at a $41 billion valuation in June 2026. Bloomberg assumes he supplied about $5.6 billion of the first round and $2 billion of the second.
blocks.whatHappened: Bezos says it is premature to disclose what it has achieved, though he calls the progress remarkable. Bloomberg values his stake at about $12 billion.
blocks.lesson: Past success lets you skip the hard part of fundraising, not the hard part of building. Judge this one only when it ships.

blocks.text: Two more long bets are still running inside Amazon. Zoox, the self-driving startup bought in 2020 for a reported $1 billion or more, now charges for robotaxi rides in Las Vegas and operates in 12 US cities. Amazon Leo, its satellite internet network, is due to begin first service later this year. Neither has yet proved it can make money.

Add it all up and a pattern appears. The ideas that lasted were ones where Amazon owned a hard skill, like logistics, cloud computing or a loyal customer base. __The flops were mostly attempts to enter someone else's market with nothing special to offer.__
Before your next idea, ask what unfair skill you already have.
The money ladder

Forget the legend for a minute and read the filing. Amazon's 1997 registration statement, the document a company must file before selling shares to the public, lists every early money move. In July 1994 Bezos bought 10.2 million shares for ==$10,000==. That is about a tenth of a cent per share.

He then lent the company $15,000, $29,000 and $40,000, with no interest, and it paid him back. He also personally guaranteed its bank merchant accounts and its company credit cards. So if Amazon failed, the bills would have come to him. He was not just the founder. In those first months he was the bank.

items.label: Bezos's own money for 10.2 million founder shares, July 1994
From his parents in two purchases, Feb and July 1995
From around 20 angels, 1995 and early 1996
From Kleiner Perkins, June 1996

blocks.text: The family money did not arrive as one big cheque. The filing shows Miguel Bezos buying 582,528 shares in February 1995. In July, a family trust led by his mother Jacklyn bought 847,716 shares. Both paid $0.1717 a share, and the two purchases add up to $245,573. His brother and sister each bought 30,000 shares in May 1996 at $0.3333.
Filings beat folklore. Always read the boring document.

Then he went looking for strangers, and that was brutal. Bezos told Congress that it took more than 50 meetings to raise $1 million, and that the most common question was what the internet was. Investors put in about $50,000 each for a little under 1 percent. Together they got about 20 percent of the company.

Tom Alberg, a former McCaw Cellular executive, was one who said yes. He remembered a friend walking away because Bezos priced the company at $6 million before the new money. Bezos would not budge, and the raise dragged on through nearly all of 1995. Brad Stone's account has another backer talking him down to $5 million. The filing shows Alberg paying $0.3333 a share for 150,000 shares, which is $50,000.

For example: in 2016 Bezos worked out what those small early cheques could have become. A $50,000 stake held to that date, if never diluted, would have been worth about $3.5 billion, a return of 70,000 times. In practice, later rounds dilute early investors, meaning each share becomes a smaller slice as new shares are sold.
The garage

The first home was a rented three-bedroom house in Bellevue, with desks built from Home Depot doors in the garage. The servers needed so much power that he and MacKenzie could not run a hair dryer or a vacuum without blowing a fuse. Early meetings were held at a local Barnes & Noble, which was the company they planned to beat.

The site opened on 16 July 1995. A bell rang for every order, and staff crowded round to check it was not somebody's mother. Within days it was too annoying, so they switched it off. Orders hit $12,000 in the first week and $14,000 in the second, and by the end of the first month they had come from all 50 states and 45 countries.

For example: one customer in Bulgaria had internet access but no credit card. He mailed cash, hidden inside a floppy disk, and explained that customs inspectors stole money but could not read English. Inside were two crisp $100 bills. Bezos told this story himself in 2010.

They had no real warehouse then. Everyone spent the second half of the day packing books on their knees on a cement floor. Bezos suggested kneepads. Someone more experienced suggested packing tables, and output rose by 20 percent. Amazon did not stock most books at first; it ordered them from distributors, and Ingram supplied 59 percent of its purchases in 1996.
He thought kneepads. Someone else said tables. Listen to the floor.
Two venture firms and a choice

Sales went from $511,000 in 1995 to $15.7 million in 1996. Venture capitalists, the professional investors who fund risky startups in exchange for shares, began to call. General Atlantic proposed a complicated price tied to whether and when Amazon went public. Kleiner Perkins offered a simple $60 million valuation. Bezos took the simple one.

The filing gives the exact deal: 569,396 preferred shares at $14.05, or ==$8 million==, signed on 21 June 1996. Preferred shares are a special class that turned into six ordinary shares each at the IPO, so Kleiner really paid about $2.34 per ordinary share. That was seven times Alberg's price from six months earlier. John Doerr joined the board.

Here is the detail almost nobody mentions. As part of that deal, Bezos gave Amazon the right to buy back 612,000 of his own shares at a tenth of a cent each if his job ended in certain circumstances. That right faded over 36 months. __Even the founder was put on a vesting schedule, which means earning your shares by staying.__ The filing ties it directly to the Kleiner round.
Founders: expect this clause. Read it, and do not take it personally.

The money changed the mood. Staff grew from 11 to 151 during 1996, and a new slogan went on the T-shirts: Get Big Fast. Early engineer Greg Linden remembered designing for four times the current load and hitting it within months. Bezos's logic was that Barnes & Noble would come online eventually, and Amazon had to be big enough by then.

He did not get rich on salary. The filing lists his pay as $64,333, with no bonus and no options. The company's total losses so far were $6 million. The risk section even admits that it depended heavily on Bezos and held no key-person life insurance, a policy that pays out if a vital leader dies.
He owned nearly half the company and paid himself $64,333.
Going public

An IPO, or initial public offering, is when a private company first sells shares to anyone on a stock exchange. Amazon filed in March 1997, assuming a price of $13 a share and 2.5 million shares. By 15 May it sold 3 million shares at ==$18== and raised $54 million, at a market value of about $438 million.

The filing said Bezos would own about 43 percent, and his family another 10 percent, on the first draft of the deal. The bigger final deal brought his share to about 41 percent. His 9.885 million shares were worth roughly $178 million at the offer price. Kleiner's $8 million had turned into about $61.5 million on paper in 11 months.

The Scott Cook detail is worth noticing too. Cook, the co-founder of Intuit, and Patricia Stonesifer, a former senior Microsoft executive, each paid $100,000 for preferred shares in early 1997, joined the board and received stock options. Bezos was collecting people who had already built big things.

Barnes & Noble, the giant of the trade, answered with lawyers. Days before the IPO it sued over the slogan Earth's Biggest Bookstore. Amazon countersued, and in October the two settled with no damages paid and no liability admitted. A barnesandnoble.com employee later told WIRED that suing Amazon just was not cool. Analysts branded the company Amazon.toast all the same.

For example: one $18 share from the IPO became 240 shares after four splits, in 1998, twice in 1999 and in 2022. A split cuts a share into more pieces without changing the total value. At the 30 October 2026 closing price of $240.35, that single share is worth about ==$57,684==, by our arithmetic.

blocks.text: Borrowing billions

Once it was public, Amazon discovered that Wall Street would lend it almost anything. In 1998 CFO Joy Covey raised $326 million in junk bonds, the first such issue by an internet company, with no payments due for five years. Junk bonds are loans to risky companies at high interest. This one yielded 10 percent.

Then came January 1999. Amazon asked for $500 million in convertible bonds and got ==$1.25 billion== the same day, because lenders kept offering. A convertible bond is a loan that the lender can swap for shares if the stock rises enough, in this case at about $156. So Amazon was paying 4.75 percent, and it did not even say what the money was for.

It spent fast. In 1998 and 1999 it put $429 million into warehouses and systems, and by late 1999 it reportedly had 70 to 80 percent more capacity than it needed. Its chief accounting officer warned Bezos that at this rate it would not be profitable for decades. In May 1999, Barron's ran a cover story calling the company Amazon.bomb.
Easy money is the most dangerous kind. It hides your mistakes.

Then came the decision that saved the company, and Bezos did not make it alone. New CFO Warren Jenson, who arrived in September 1999, feared suppliers might demand faster payment if confidence cracked. Advised by Morgan Stanley's Ruth Porat, he went to Europe in February 2000 and sold about $672 million of convertible bonds at nearly 7 percent. It was an expensive deal.

The Nasdaq peaked on 10 March, about a month later. Brad Stone reported that the deal could not have gone through just three weeks later, and that without that cushion Amazon would almost certainly have faced insolvency, meaning it could not pay its debts. __The best time to raise money is when you do not need it, because the door can shut without warning.__

For example: here is why cash mattered so much. A customer paid Amazon for a book immediately, but Amazon paid the supplier up to about 90 days later. So growth actually pumped cash into the company. If suppliers got nervous and demanded quicker payment, that pump would run in reverse, and fast.
The analyst who said it would die

On 22 June 2000 a young Lehman Brothers bond analyst named Ravi Suria published a report that spread everywhere. He called Amazon's credit extremely weak and deteriorating, and said it would run out of cash within four quarters unless it pulled another financing rabbit from its hat. Its 4.75 percent bonds fell from about $75 to $58 in days, and the stock dropped about 20 percent in one day.

Bezos hit back on stage at PC Expo in New York days later. He told a crowd of nearly 1,000 that the analyst had not even called the company, and that Amazon had a billion dollars in cash. Behind the scenes, he, Jenson and treasurer Russ Grandinetti flew around reassuring suppliers. If the suppliers had panicked, the prediction could have come true by itself.

Suria kept going. In February 2001 he warned of a creditor squeeze in the second half of the year. His numbers were real: Amazon's working capital, its short-term assets minus short-term debts, had fallen to $386 million from over $700 million. Its shareholders' equity had gone to negative $967 million. Amazon's spokesman called it a silly report and said Suria had already missed his first prediction by $1.1 billion.

blocks.text: Bezos opened his letter to shareholders for 2000 with one word: Ouch. His own fortune shrank with the stock, from over $9 billion in mid-1999 to about $1.7 billion by 2003. Pundits thought Amazon was going out of business. But he also argued that the company was stronger than ever, and that a falling share price was not a failing business.
The stock fell over 90 percent. He kept shipping. Separate price from business.
The cuts and the coffee

Survival needed real pain. In January 2001 Amazon cut 1,300 jobs, closed a warehouse in McDonough, Georgia, shut a Seattle customer service centre, and took a charge of over $150 million. It also stopped selling items that lost money. Bezos had resisted running to Wall Street's expectations, but the bust forced his hand.

It also rented out what it had built. In August 2000 it signed a 10-year deal to run the online toy store for Toysrus.com, handling the site, fulfilment and customer service. Borders followed in 2001, and Internet News reported $125 million coming in from Toys R Us after one Christmas. That excess warehouse space had started earning. In July 2001 AOL put ==$100 million== into Amazon shares.

That same year Bezos had coffee with Jim Sinegal, the founder of Costco, at a Starbucks inside a Barnes & Noble. He had come to talk about buying goods wholesale. Sinegal instead explained how Costco kept prices so low that members saw the value every time they walked in. Days later, Stone reports, Bezos called a meeting on Amazon's incoherent pricing. To be fair, Bezos has never publicly credited that coffee.

That summer Amazon cut book, music and video prices by up to 30 percent, while its cost cuts paid for it. Then, on 22 January 2002, came results that almost nobody had predicted. Sales for the last quarter of 2001 were $1.12 billion, its first billion-dollar quarter. Net profit was ==$5 million==, or one cent a share.
One cent per share. Seven years in. Celebrate your small wins.

In the same announcement he introduced Super Saver Shipping, free on orders over $99, as an everyday offer and not a promotion. He had just scraped into profit, and he gave the money straight back to customers. Bezos said there were two kinds of retailer, those working to raise prices and those working to lower them, and that Amazon had chosen the second.

So was Suria wrong? He was wrong about the outcome, and by then he had left for a hedge fund. But Commoncog's case study makes a fair point: he had correctly spotted a real weakness, and the company survived partly because of a bond sale that closed just in time. Stone called it a mix of conviction, improvisation and luck. __Never let a good outcome convince you there was no danger.__

blocks.text: Most companies that nearly die become careful. Amazon did the opposite. Within six years of its first profit, it launched a shipping club that would be expensive at first, a cloud business that outsiders called a distraction and a device that could wreck its own book sales. Here is what those decisions looked like from inside the room.
The boathouse

It began with an annoyance. Engineer Charlie Ward loved 1-Click ordering, but it did not work with free shipping, and that irritated him more and more. He wondered aloud whether customers might pay a lump sum each year and never see a shipping charge again. His colleagues paused, wondering if he was crazy, so he wrote it up in half a page and used the employee suggestion box.

Late in 2004 Bezos took it up. One Friday in December, the team cancelled a meeting with him because the site had crashed for hours. He understood, then told them to come over on Saturday morning anyway. They were sent to the boathouse at his home, which one of them remembers as bigger than his own apartment. Bezos wanted a moat around Amazon's best customers.

He gave them four weeks. They said six was the minimum. So he moved the date of a quarterly earnings call by about two weeks to fit, which is not a thing CEOs usually do for a side project. The team printed T-shirts saying it would ship in six weeks or less, and left one behind whenever they poached an engineer from another team.

For example: two-day delivery cost $9.48 an order back then, so Prime at $79 paid for itself in nine orders. Amazon weighed $49 and $99 before Bezos chose. An insider later said it was never really about the $79. It was about changing how people thought, so that they stopped shopping around.
An engineer's half-page became a business with 100 million-plus US customers.
The side project nobody understood

AWS started as a cleanup job. Around 2000, Amazon tried to run online shops for other retailers and found its code was a mess, so it split its systems into clean building blocks. Projects still took too long because every team built its own storage and computing. Then, at a 2003 offsite at Bezos's home, a 30-minute exercise on what the company was good at ran long.

The answer surprised them. To survive on thin retail margins, they had become very good at cheap, reliable data centres. Jassy got the job of turning that into a business. By late 2004 a tiny team was in Cape Town, working thousands of miles from headquarters because its leader wanted to go home. It built the computing service almost independently of Seattle.

Observers called it a risky distraction. Bezos remembered them asking what storage had to do with selling books. It launched in 2006, charging by use, so a startup with a credit card could rent what used to require millions of dollars of its own servers. Rivals took years to respond. __Amazon's great advantage was that for years nobody thought a bookshop was serious competition in computing.__

Then Amazon kept quiet about how well it was going. It stayed silent on the unit's numbers until 2015, when it finally reported them. Even then the quarterly operating profit of over $250 million surprised people, at about 17 percent margins, against 2 to 3 percent in retail. By then its lead was already large.

blocks.text: Kill your own business

In 2004 books were at the heart of Amazon, and Apple was showing with the iPod how fast a media business could move to a device. So Bezos reassigned Steve Kessel, the man running books, and told him his job was to destroy that business. Asked for a deadline, Bezos said he was already late, according to Brad Stone.

Bezos then did something most leaders would not dare. He priced most e-books at $9.99 at launch, a number one case study traces to Apple's 99-cent songs, not to any margin calculation. The team tested prototypes during a weekend away with him, reading for an hour and then discussing how the device felt in the hand. Kessel told him it would take 18 months. It took three and a half years.
He attacked his own best business before anyone else could.
Failing at the right size

Fire Phone was the expensive embarrassment. In October 2014 Amazon took its $170 million charge, and hedge fund manager David Einhorn told investors that Amazon's story was breaking: growth was slowing, and losses were growing. It was the biggest quarterly loss in 14 years. The critics seemed to have a point.

Freed, a key leader on the phone, might have expected to take the blame. According to The New Yorker, Bezos told him he must not lose one minute of sleep over it. Earlier, during a demo of the phone's software, Bezos had asked it for Hotel California. When the song played, he was delighted, and soon asked Freed to build a cloud computer you could talk to. Four months after the phone, Echo arrived.

Dave Limp, who ran devices, later said that if you had listened to the skeptics you would have cancelled both products. In his 2018 letter Bezos wrote that Amazon's experiments should grow with the company, even to multibillion-dollar failures. He said Fire Phone's lessons and developers sped up Echo and Alexa. __The team that failed was kept, and that is why the next try was possible.__
Keep the team after a failure. They just paid for the lesson.
The deals

Amazon also bought what it could not build. The shoe seller Zappos came in 2009, the warehouse robot maker Kiva in 2012 for $775 million, and the game-streaming site Twitch in 2014 at a reported $970 million. PillPack in 2018 pushed it into pharmacy. MGM, the James Bond studio, was agreed in 2021 for $8.45 billion. By then Bezos had already announced he was stepping aside as CEO.

The biggest was Whole Foods. CEO John Mackey said publicly that it was love at first sight after a blind date in Seattle. The filings tell a tougher story. Amazon offered $41 a share and warned that it would walk away if word leaked or if Whole Foods shopped the deal. Whole Foods asked for $45, and Amazon said $42 was final. Whole Foods took it.

For example: Ring began as Doorbot, a video doorbell pitched on the TV show Shark Tank in 2013. Founder Jamie Siminoff asked for $700,000, was turned down by every Shark but one, refused that offer and ended up in tears, almost out of money. Five years later Amazon bought the company at a reported $1 billion or more.
Hundreds of investors rejected Ring. Rejection is data, not a verdict.
Who he beat, and who beat him

The honest scorecard is mixed. Against book chains he won clearly. He ended up running Borders' website from 2001, and Barnes & Noble's attack in court gave way to Amazon's own patent suit against it over 1-Click in 1999. He also built a cloud business years before rivals responded.

But he lost phones to Apple and Samsung, and China to Alibaba and JD.com. India remains unfinished, with Flipkart still ahead on gross sales at last count. In space, SpaceX got its big NASA lander deal first in 2021, Blue Origin winning a $3.4 billion lander contract only in 2023. Walmart bought both Jet.com and Flipkart, and became a stronger rival.

Amazon crossed a market value of ==$1 trillion== for the first time in September 2018. In February 2021, Bezos told staff he would hand the CEO job to Jassy that summer and focus on Day One, Earth Fund, Blue Origin and The Washington Post. It ended 27 years in the job, and began the next stage of his working life.
